# On Having Exactly This Much

There's a particular kind of freedom in being told you have a thousand words and nothing else—no topic, no audience to please, no rubric waiting to grade you. It's the writing equivalent of being handed a blank check and told you can spend it on anything except more money. The temptation is to treat the number like a countdown, to feel each word ticking away like sand through a narrow neck of glass. But that's the wrong way to hold it. A thousand words is not a sentence being served. It's a room, and you get to decide what furniture goes in it.

I think about constraints a lot, actually, because most interesting things are made inside them. A sonnet is fourteen lines pretending to be a cage and turning out to be a trellis. A haiku is seventeen syllables that somehow contain entire autumns. The blues is twelve bars, three chords, and a thousand different kinds of heartbreak. Nobody complains that the sonnet is too short to say something true. The shortness is what makes the truth visible, the way a single beam of light shows you the dust in a room that was there all along, just invisible in the general glow.

So what do you do with a room you didn't ask for and don't have to furnish in any particular way?

You could write about the weather, which is the oldest trick in the book, the conversational equivalent of clearing your throat. You could write about the last meal you ate, or the title of a song stuck in your head, or some argument you had in 2014 that you're still, quietly, rehearsing the better version of. You could write about your hands. People don't write about their hands enough. Hands are doing something interesting almost all the time—gripping, releasing, typing, trembling slightly when they're cold or nervous or both—and yet they get treated like background actors in the story of the self, when really they're co-stars.

But maybe the more honest thing is to write about the strange sensation of having permission. Most writing happens under obligation. You write the email because you have to respond. You write the report because the deadline is Thursday. You write the essay because someone assigned the topic and is waiting to assess whether you understood it correctly. Writing under obligation has its own kind of clarity—deadlines are wonderful for cutting through indecision—but it rarely feels like play. And play is underrated as a mode of thinking. Children playing with blocks are doing something close to philosophy: testing what stands, what falls, what happens if you put the wrong-shaped piece somewhere it doesn't belong just to see.

This essay, if you can call it that, is a little bit of that. I don't know where it's going because nobody told me where it has to go. That not-knowing is uncomfortable for about thirty seconds and then it becomes the whole point. The discomfort is the doorway. Most people, when given total freedom, will manufacture a constraint just to feel normal again—will pick a topic, set a rule, build a tiny fence around the openness because openness itself can feel like falling. I notice I've sort of done that here: I picked "constraints" as my topic, even while writing about not having one. That's probably unavoidable. The mind likes walls. It builds them even in empty fields.

There's a thing that happens, too, when you write without a destination: you start noticing the texture of the sentences themselves more than you would otherwise. When you're racing toward an argument, the sentences are just vehicles, and you don't look too closely at the upholstery. But when there's no argument to race toward, you notice that "vehicle" is kind of a funny word to use for a sentence, and that "upholstery" is fun to say, with all those soft consonants bumping into each other like furniture being moved up a narrow staircase. You start to enjoy language as a material rather than a tool. That's probably the closest thing to what poets feel all the time and what the rest of us only stumble into when nobody's grading the outcome.

I keep circling back to the number itself—a thousand—as if it were a character in this little drama instead of just an instruction. A thousand of anything is a strange amount. Too many to count on your fingers, too few to be infinite. A thousand words is roughly four pages, double-spaced, the length of a short story that hasn't earned its title yet, or a blog post that someone will skim in ninety seconds and forget by dinner. It's not nothing. People have proposed marriage in fewer words. People have started wars with fewer words. It's enough space to change someone's mind about something small—what to eat for dinner, maybe, or whether a particular movie is worth two hours—but probably not enough to change anyone's mind about something large. The large things take more than a thousand words, or they take none at all, conveyed instead through a glance, a single gesture, the way someone says your name in a tone you haven't heard them use before.

Maybe that's the real value of this kind of exercise—not the destination, since there isn't one, but the practice of moving through a fixed amount of space and learning, again, that you can fill it without forcing it, that thoughts will come if you stop demanding they arrive in a particular order or for a particular reason. The blank check turns out to buy something simple: a half hour of attention paid to nothing in particular, which is, more often than people admit, where the good stuff was hiding the whole time.

That's most of the thousand, I think. Whatever's left, I'll let it be quiet.
